say.en: Your wishes are the indifference map; your wallet is the budget line. Put them on the same graph and the best choice appears. In this lesson: State the condition for consumer's equilibrium (MRS equals p 1 over p 2).
Explain why points of intersection are not optimal.

body.en: A rational consumer chooses the bundle on the budget line that lies on the highest possible indifference curve. At this optimum the budget line is tangent to an indifference curve, so the slope of the IC equals the slope of the budget line: $MRS = p_1/p_2$. The *consumer's* own rate of exchange equals the market's rate of exchange.

body.en: If MRS > p₁/p₂, the *consumer* values good 1 more than the market charges, so buying more of good 1 (and less of good 2) moves him to a higher indifference curve. If MRS < p₁/p₂, he gains by buying more of good 2. Only at tangency can no affordable change raise satisfaction. In utility analysis the same idea appears as the law of equi-marginal utility: $MU_x/P_x = MU_y/P_y$.

problem.en: Px = ₹2, Py = ₹3, income = ₹12. MU of X for units 1–5: 20, 16, 12, 8, 4. MU of Y: 24, 18, 12, 6, 3. Find the equilibrium bundle.

steps.en: Equal MU per rupee = 6 at 3 units of X and 2 units of Y.

answer.en: Equilibrium: 3 units of X and 2 units of Y (MUx/Px = MUy/Py = 6).

narration.en: Let us work this out together. Px = ₹2, Py = ₹3, income = ₹12. MU of X for units 1–5: 20, 16, 12, 8, 4. MU of Y: 24, 18, 12, 6, 3. Find the equilibrium bundle.

say.en: Let us work this out together. Px equals 2, rupees Py equals 3, rupees income equals 12 rupees. MU of X for units 1-5: 20, 16, 12, 8, 4. MU of Y: 24, 18, 12, 6, 3. Find the equilibrium bundle.
MU per rupee for X divided by 2: 10, 8, 6, 4, 2.
MU per rupee for Y divided by 3: 8, 6, 4, 2, 1.
Equal MU per rupee equals 6 at 3 units of X and 2 units of Y.
Cost: 3 times 2 plus 2 times 3 equals 12 rupees equals income. Both conditions hold.
So the answer is Equilibrium: 3 units of X and 2 units of Y (MUx/Px equals MUy/Py equals 6).
